Spanish police used excessive force during general strike, Amnesty says

By Meriem Tourabi MADRID, Nov 20 (Reuters) – Spanish police used excessive force against protesters and journalists during last week’s general strike, rights group Amnesty International said on Friday.

• Amnesty said police used pepper spray, batons, tear gas and rubber bullets, and left 36 people injured, 5 of them hospitalised

• The NGO said it had documented incidents in Barcelona, Malaga, Valencia, Alicante and Granada, as well as Madrid, where it said demonstrators were not given any warning before police charged

Show Full Article

• Asked for comment by Reuters, the Interior Ministry pointed to its announcement the day after the strike that the use of pepper spray during demonstrations would be curbed

• Madrid police authorities on Thursday opened an internal investigation to assess officers’ actions in the capital

• Journalists were pushed and hit with batons while covering the strike, Amnesty said

• The group said its findings were based on interviews with 24 people. It called on authorities to carry out an “in-depth review of the protocols and rules that regulate police action at demonstrations”

(Reporting by Meriem Tourabi; Editing by David Latona and Andrew Heavens)

MADRID, Nov 20 (Reuters) – Spain’s High Court has released pro-Palestinian donor and US media heir James Cox Chambers Jr. on conditional bail, while it considers an extradition request by the United States, according to a court ruling released on Friday.

The court said it had decided to release Chambers after US authorities acknowledged what they described as substantial and unintentional errors in the Spanish translation of an FBI agent’s sworn statement submitted in support of the extradition request.

Chambers, whose family owns Cox Enterprises, was arrested at the request of US authorities on July 10 while on holiday in Ibiza. He has been held in custody since on accusations including riot, conspiracy to commit riot and international money laundering. Chambers, known as Fergie, denies wrongdoing.

Show Full Article

After a hearing last week, the court had been expected to rule on the extradition request in the coming weeks, but it said on Friday that the translation errors could delay a final decision.

Judges said the issue could be relevant to the outcome of the proceedings because it raised questions about the accuracy of documents provided by US authorities and could weaken, at least temporarily, the basis for the extradition request.

Chambers must report weekly to a local court, surrender his passport, remain in Spain, provide an address and appear before the High Court whenever summoned.

The case is politically sensitive for Spain’s Socialist-led government, whose strong pro-Palestinian stance has drawn criticism from the administration of US President Donald Trump and added to wider tensions with Washington.

If the court approves the extradition, Spain’s cabinet will make the final decision.

Separately, Chambers’ lawyers said they were challenging a raid by Irish police on his family home in Dublin, which they said was conducted at the request of US authorities and involved the seizure of electronic devices and other property. His legal team said it would seek judicial review unless authorities clarify the legal basis for the operation.

(Reporting by Emma Pinedo, additional reporting by Kate Holton, editing by Andrei Khalip and Sharon Singleton)
